# E-1899 — Remove the unused list tree

A removal checklist, not a design. The only risk in this task is deleting the
wrong `--tree`: there are four flags by that name and two identically-named
glyph maps, and the two flags you must NOT touch are the ones actually in use.

> **Amended during implementation.** Three things landed that this plan did not
> anticipate; each is marked ⊕ below.
>
> 1. A **third bare `tree` reference** in `show_plan` — the sort default —
>    which the site table missed. Mechanical.
> 2. A **doc line** in `docs/guide/tasks.md` advertising the removed flag.
> 3. The **second `status_indicators` map was deleted too**, reversing this
>    plan's "Do NOT touch" directive. It turned out to be dead code. See
>    *Reversal* below; filed and closed as E-1924.

## One renderer, two flags

`epic_cmd.list_epics` is a thin wrapper that forwards `tree=tree` into
`task_cmd.show_plan` with `type_filter="epic"`. So `task list --tree` and
`epic list --tree` share a single implementation — there is ONE branch and ONE
glyph map to delete, not two.

## Remove

| Site | What |
|---|---|
| `cli.py:1225` | the `--tree/as_tree` option on `task list` |
| `cli.py:2521` | the `--tree/as_tree` option on `epic list` |
| `cli.py` (both bodies) | the `tree=as_tree` argument passed onward |
| `epic_cmd.list_epics` | the `tree` parameter and its pass-through to `show_plan` |
| `task_cmd.show_plan` | the `tree` parameter |
| `task_cmd.show_plan` | the `else: # Tree output` branch — the `by_id` / `children_of` / `_render` block, ending at the `_render(None, 1)` call |
| `task_cmd.py` ~:1100 | the `status_indicators` map that opens that branch |
| ⊕ `task_cmd.show_plan` | the sort default `if not tree and not sort_by:` → `if not sort_by:` |
| ⊕ `docs/guide/tasks.md:34` | the `endless task list --tree # hierarchical` line |
| ⊕ `task_cmd.next_tasks` ~:1209 | the second `status_indicators` map — see *Reversal* |

After removal, `show_plan`'s `if not tree: _render_flat_table(rows)` collapses
to an unconditional `_render_flat_table(rows)`; the trailing `click.echo()` and
the `N item(s)` summary below the branch stay.

⊕ The site table above missed a third bare `tree` reference: `show_plan` picked
its ORDER BY with `if not tree and not sort_by: sort_by = "id"`, falling through
to `pi.sort_order` for the tree. Removing the parameter leaves `if not sort_by`.
Flat ordering is unchanged — the flat path always defaulted to id. A `NameError`
on the first `task list` after the branch deletion is what surfaced it.

## ⊕ Reversal — the second glyph map went too

This plan told the implementer to preserve the `status_indicators` map in
`next_tasks` as an unrelated bystander. That was wrong: the map is **dead
code**. It is assigned and never read — `next_tasks` renders through
`_render_flat_table`, which has no glyph column. `grep -n 'indicator'
task_cmd.py` returned only the assignment line.

So the resolution is deletion, not preservation. Adding a glyph column to
`task next` to make the map live would be an unrequested behavior change;
`task next` output is byte-for-byte what it was. Filed as E-1924
(`cleans_up` E-1899), then folded into this task's commit and closed obsolete.

Consequence for the framing at the top of this plan: there were two
identically-named glyph maps and **both** are gone. The "don't delete the wrong
one" hazard is now only about the four `--tree` flags.

## Do NOT touch

- **`session status --tree`** (`cli.py:815`) and **`session monitor --tree`**
  (`cli.py:839`). These are the trees actually in use. They are Go-backed
  (`internal/sessionstatuscmd`), reach the renderer through
  `session_status_resolve`, and share nothing with the list tree but the flag
  name.

## Verification — `tests/tasks/e-1899-verify.sh`

Author the script; it is the deliverable the user runs. Hand back exactly one
command:

```
esu && ./tests/tasks/e-1899-verify.sh
```

Copy the harness shape from `tests/tasks/e-1845-verify.sh` (the `report_pass` /
`report_fail` / `assert_*` / `summary` block and the isolated-fixture setup:
throwaway git repo, temp `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`/`XDG_CACHE_HOME`, worktree `bin` on
PATH). E-1623 will retrofit these onto a shared harness later; until then match
the current shape rather than inventing a new one.

**A — fail-fast gate.** `uv run pytest tests/ -q` passes. A removal must not
break an unrelated suite, and there is no point running the rest if it did.
Abort the run on failure.

**B — the flags are gone.** `endless task list --tree` and
`endless epic list --tree` both fail as unknown options, and their `--help`
output no longer lists `--tree`.

**C — the flat table is untouched.** `endless task list` and
`endless epic list` still render, and `--status`, `--phase`, `--sort`, `--llm`,
and `--json` all still behave. Seed a small task tree with parents and children
so a regression in the flat renderer would actually show.

**D — the trees that matter still work.** `endless session status --tree` and
`endless session monitor --tree` still render. This is the check that catches
the one dangerous failure mode of this task: deleting the wrong `--tree`. Assert
against real output, not just an exit code.

**E — ⊕ both glyph maps are gone and `task next` is unchanged.** As written this
check asserted that `endless task next` "still renders its status glyphs" —
a false premise: it never rendered them, which is exactly how the map was found
to be dead. Reframed to the guarantee that actually holds: no `status_indicators`
survives in `task_cmd.py`, nothing reads an `indicator`, and `task next` still
renders its header, column heads, rows, `--json` and `--llm` exactly as before.

**F — no dangling references.** Grep the tree for `tree=` and `as_tree` in
`src/endless`; the only survivors should be the two `session_status_resolve`
call sites. Nothing should still pass `tree` to `show_plan` or `list_epics`.

**⊕ G — project-wide regression.** `go test ./...` passes. The Python suite is
already the section-A gate; this is its Go counterpart, run at the end.

## Not in scope

An interactive TUI tree — what is actually wanted instead of this — is a much
larger piece of work and is deliberately unfiled.

## Note for E-1891

The deleted glyph map is the per-row lookup cited in E-1891's plan as the one
place worth measuring for subprocess cost. Landing this first dissolves that
concern rather than answering it. ⊕ Doubly so: both maps are now gone, so
whichever of the two E-1891 meant, there is nothing left to measure.

# Plan — E-1893: require replies to restate the task IDs they are about

## Decisions (user, 2026-08-08)

Delivery surfaces: **handoff templates, the E-1919 output style, and `endless guide`**.
Explicitly NOT the E-1803 PostToolUse nudge — E-1911 just rewrote that nudge and parked
E-1901's enforcement arm, so it is recently-settled ground this task will not disturb.

The style's reach gap is closed two ways: activate it for endless now, and add a
**dim FYI on stderr** telling a *human* operator the style is installed but inactive.
Optional in principle; treated as required for any project using Endless for now.

## Part 1 — handoff templates (one sentence, one place)

The analysis's open question (a line in each of seven templates vs a shared fragment)
resolves itself: `internal/templatecmd/templates/handoff/_close.tmpl` already exists,
already holds the reporting instructions, and is already parsed into every handoff
template's set via `handoffPartialNames`. Add the rule to the `handoff_close` define.

Wording must cover the crux from the analysis — the subject is often NOT the session's
own task, so the tmux window title does not supply the missing ID:

> Name the explicit task ID(s) in the first sentence that makes a claim about a task —
> including tasks other than your own, where my window title tells me nothing.

Do NOT add it to `handoff_verify` / `handoff_nonverify`; those are about the verify
command, and duplicating the rule invites drift between copies.

## Part 2 — E-1919 output style

The style's `## Lead with the IDs` section already says to open with the bare
identifiers the answer concerns. It does not stress the other-tasks case, which the
analysis calls the crux. Strengthen that section only — do not restructure it.

Because the style file is embedded, the change is made in
`internal/outputstylecmd/templates/Endless.md.tmpl`, then re-materialized into
`.claude/output-styles/Endless.md` with `outputstyle install --force`. Both copies must
be committed; a stale committed copy would silently shadow the intent.

`tests/tasks/e-1919-verify.sh` section 8 asserts the style body's contract clauses. Add
an assertion for the other-tasks wording so this cannot regress.

## Part 3 — `endless guide`

Add the rule to the reporting guidance in the guide's orchestration/reporting section,
for sessions not started from a handoff. Keep it to the same one sentence used in
`_close.tmpl` — three surfaces carrying three paraphrases is how the rule drifts.

Re-run `just regenerate-guide` if the section map changes.

## Part 4 — activate the style for endless

Commit `"outputStyle": "Endless"` into the main checkout's tracked
`.claude/settings.json`. Verified safe: `just claude-settings-init` rebuilds each
worktree's settings from the committed copy's non-hook keys plus the working copy's,
replacing only `hooks` (justfile:381-385), so the key survives worktree regeneration
rather than being dropped.

Note this is a genuine behavior change for every endless session, which is why E-1919
made it opt-in. It is being opted into deliberately here, not by default.

## Part 5 — the dim FYI (human-only, stderr, appended)

**Trigger:** any `endless` command run by a human. Never when run by an agent.

**Detection already exists — twice.** `agent_help.is_claude_code_agent()` and
`task_cmd._running_under_agent()` are byte-identical (`CLAUDECODE == "1"`). Consolidate
onto `agent_help.is_claude_code_agent()` and delete the duplicate rather than adding a
third caller — same reasoning that folded `templatecmd` onto
`monitor.ProjectRootFromCwd` in E-1919.

**Behavior:**
- Fires only when `not is_claude_code_agent()`.
- Fires only when the project has the style file present but `outputStyle` unset (or set
  to something else) in `.claude/settings.json` — i.e. exactly the inert state
  `outputstyle install` warns about.
- Writes to **stderr**, dim, appended after the command's normal output, so it never
  corrupts stdout for pipes/`--json` consumers.
- One line. Not an error, not a non-zero exit.
- Suppressed when the project has no style file at all (nothing to activate) and when
  `.claude/settings.json` is unreadable.

**Wording:** dim, and it must name the activation route, since there is no
`/output-style` command:

> FYI: the Endless output style is installed but not active — `/config output-style=Endless`

**Throttle:** must not print on every command in a tight loop. Reuse the existing
activity-throttle shape (`monitor.ShouldThrottle`) or an equivalent once-per-N-minutes
marker under the cache dir. Decide at implementation time; do NOT ship an unthrottled
per-invocation nag — that is the noise failure that got E-1901's gate parked.

**Placement:** a single hook in the Python CLI's result callback / group teardown so it
appends after any subcommand, rather than being pasted into individual commands.

## Verification

Fold into the existing suite per the one-command rule:
`esu && ./tests/tasks/e-1893-verify.sh`

Checks:
1. `handoff_close` renders the ID rule for every handoff type (todo, bugfix, research,
   epic, brainstorm, respawn) — asserts the shared partial actually reaches all of them.
2. The rule appears exactly once per rendered handoff, not once per template that
   includes a partial.
3. The style body carries the other-tasks wording.
4. The embedded template and the committed `.claude/output-styles/Endless.md` are
   byte-identical — catches a re-materialization that was forgotten.
5. `endless guide` output contains the rule.
6. The FYI fires with `CLAUDECODE` unset and a project in the inert state.
7. The FYI does NOT fire when `CLAUDECODE=1`.
8. The FYI does NOT fire when `outputStyle` is already `Endless`.
9. The FYI goes to stderr, not stdout: stdout of a `--json` command still parses.
10. The FYI does not change exit status.
11. Only one agent-detection helper remains in the Python source.

## Out of scope

- The E-1803 PostToolUse nudge (user decision).
- A `--global` output style install; E-1919's project-scoped decision stands. If the
  per-project activation proves too narrow across 50+ sessions, that is a separate
  change against E-1785, not this task.
- Any enforcement gate. This task delivers instructions on three surfaces plus one
  human-facing FYI; it deliberately adds no teeth.

# Plan — E-1915: refuse to remove a task that still has relations

`task remove` orphans `task_deps` rows, and reused ids resurrect them. The fix is
a guard, not a cascade.

## The decision: deny on all six, no exemptions

`task remove` REFUSES while any `task_deps` row references the task, and names
the rows so the operator can clear them. It does not delete relations as a side
effect of deleting a task.

Deny rather than cascade because a severed relation is unrecoverable and a
refusal costs one command. Cascading can be revisited if the friction proves
real; the reverse migration (discovering months later that a chain was silently
severed) has no fix.

All six types, including `relates_to`, with no per-type exemption. `relates_to`
is the weakest relation and was the obvious candidate to auto-delete, but one
rule that always holds beats two rules with a judgment call at the boundary —
and every "harmless" exemption is a second code path that can orphan rows again.
It is one `task unlink` away. If it proves annoying in practice, relax that one
type then, with evidence.

This matches what `task remove` already does with children: it RAISES (not
warns) and tells you to pass `--cascade`. Refusing on relations is the existing
shape, not a new kind of behavior.

## No new flag. `--cascade` below is the one that already exists

`endless task remove` already has `--cascade` ("Also remove all descendants"). It
is about CHILDREN and predates this task. Nothing here adds a relations
equivalent — there is deliberately no way to remove a task and its relations in
one command, because that is the cascade this plan rejects.

It is named below only to settle WHICH tasks get checked:

- `task remove E-100` deletes one task — check E-100's relations.
- `task remove E-100 --cascade` deletes E-100 and every descendant — check all of
  their relations too.

The second case is not a nicety. If only the root were checked, the guard would
be bypassed by removing a parent instead of the child that holds the link, and
the descendants would be deleted with their relations orphaned exactly as today.

## Implementation

`remove_item` in `src/endless/task_cmd.py` (currently ~line 2260).

1. After the existing child-count check, collect the relation rows for every id
   about to be deleted:

   - Without `--cascade`, that is the one task.
   - With `--cascade`, that is the task PLUS its full descendant set. Reuse the
     `WITH RECURSIVE tree(id)` query already in the function (it is computed
     today only to print a count). This is the case most likely to have
     relations, and checking only the root would let a parent removal bypass the
     guard entirely.

   ```sql
   SELECT id, source_id, target_id, dep_type FROM task_deps
    WHERE (source_type = 'task' AND source_id  IN (<ids>))
       OR (target_type = 'task' AND target_id IN (<ids>))
    ORDER BY id
   ```

2. If any row comes back, raise `click.ClickException` listing each relation as
   the exact `task unlink` command that clears it, using the CANONICAL_DEP_TYPES
   display name and the correct source/target order:

   ```
   Task E-1914 has 3 relations. Removing it would orphan them —
   task_deps rows survive a task delete, and ids are reused, so a later
   task inheriting E-1914 would inherit these too. Unlink them first:

       endless task unlink 1914 --to 1911 --type cleans_up
       endless task unlink 1914 --to 1900 --type relates_to
       endless task unlink 1899 --to 1914 --type blocks
   ```

   Under `--cascade`, attribute each row to the descendant it belongs to, or the
   operator cannot tell which of several tasks is holding up the removal.

3. Raise BEFORE `emit_event(kind="task.deleted", ...)`. That event currently
   fires ahead of the delete; a refusal after it would publish a deletion that
   never happened.

## Also fix: the rows already orphaned

The guard stops new orphans; it does not clean up the ones the ledger has
accumulated. Add a repair that reports and deletes rows whose task endpoint no
longer exists:

```sql
SELECT * FROM task_deps
 WHERE (source_type = 'task' AND source_id NOT IN (SELECT id FROM tasks))
    OR (target_type = 'task' AND target_id NOT IN (SELECT id FROM tasks))
```

Fold it into whatever `endless reconcile` already does for consistency repair
rather than adding a new verb. Print what it removed — a silent repair of silent
corruption teaches nothing.

Note the ordering hazard: this query only finds orphans whose id is still FREE.
Any orphan whose id has already been reused is indistinguishable from a genuine
relation and cannot be recovered by query. Run the repair as part of landing
this, and accept that anything already resurrected is lost.

## Audit in the same pass

Every other table keyed on a task id has the same reuse exposure and should be
checked for the same gap — `task_landings` and `session_task_relations` at
minimum. Report what is found; fix in this task only if the fix is small,
otherwise file it.

## Verification — `tests/tasks/e-1915-verify.sh`

- Removing a task with a `blocks` relation is refused, and the message contains
  the exact `task unlink` command that clears it.
- Refused for each of the six types independently, `relates_to` included — the
  no-exemption rule is the decision, so it is the assertion.
- Refused when the task is the TARGET as well as the source (the `1899 blocks
  1914` direction), which is the half a naive `source_id = ?` check misses.
- `--cascade` is refused when a DESCENDANT holds the relation and the root holds
  none, and the message names the descendant.
- After `task unlink`, the same removal succeeds and leaves zero `task_deps`
  rows referencing the id.
- The reconcile repair deletes a hand-seeded orphan row and reports it.
- Regression: removing a task with no relations still works, and removing a task
  with children still raises the existing `--cascade` message.

# Second landing — folding in E-1927 and E-1928

Both were found while verifying the first landing and filed as follow-ups. Both
are folded back in here rather than tracked separately: neither needed a design
call once stated, and both reuse helpers the first landing already added.

## E-1927 — the other way a task gets deleted

The first landing put the guard in `remove_item`, so it only covered
`endless task remove`. Two commands delete `tasks` rows without going near it:

- `endless task import <file> --replace` → `_do_import` (`task_cmd.py`)
- `endless task import-json --clear`     → `import_json` (`task_cmd.py`)

Both emit `task.bulk_cleared`, which `execTaskBulkCleared`
(`internal/events/executor.go`) runs as
`DELETE FROM tasks WHERE project_id = ? AND source_file = ?` — no relation
cleanup, no guard. Reproduced before the fix: import a plan, link one of its
tasks, re-import with `--replace` — task gone, `task_deps` row still there.

**Decision: same rule, same refusal.** The reason to hesitate was that refusing
a *bulk file refresh* is more obstructive than refusing one named `task remove`
— the operator may not know which relation the guard means. That is answered by
the message rather than by a weaker rule: it names the file, groups every row
under the task holding it, and gives the exact `unlink`. An imported task that
has since been linked to is not disposable just because a file regenerated it,
and the relation is unrecoverable however the task went away.

No new flag. Re-import without `--replace` / `--clear` if the refresh matters
more than the relation.

Implementation: `_refuse_bulk_clear_with_relations(project_id, source_file)`
resolves the tasks that clear would delete and hands them to the existing
`_relations_referencing()`. Raised before the emit, like the remove-side guard.
The message body is now shared — `_orphan_refusal()` builds it for both call
sites, so the rule reads identically however the caller got here.

## E-1928 — `--cascade` always reported 0 descendants

Pre-existing, not introduced by the first landing; found while verifying the
cascade guard. `remove_item` emitted `task.deleted` and only THEN ran a
recursive query to count the descendants it had just deleted. `emit_event`
executes the delete synchronously, so the CTE always seeded from an empty table:

    $ endless task remove 8600 --cascade      # parent + child + grandchild
    • Removed E-8600 and 0 descendant(s): P

Fix: `_removal_id_set(item_id, cascade)` — added by the first landing for the
guard — already computes exactly that id set, before the delete. `remove_item`
now calls it once, passes it to the guard, and reports `len(removal_ids) - 1`.
The post-delete query is gone; no query was added to replace it.

## Verification — the same `tests/tasks/e-1915-verify.sh`

Folded in as new checks rather than a second script:

- Section E gains an assertion that the cascade success line reports the real
  descendant count (`and 2 descendant(s)`), not 0.
- New section E2: a re-import with `--replace` is refused while an imported
  task holds a relation; the message names the file and the clearing command;
  the task and its relation both survive the refusal; after `unlink` the same
  re-import succeeds and leaves nothing orphaned; a relation on a task the
  import does not own never blocks the refresh.
- `tests/test_task_remove_relations.py` gains unit coverage for
  `_refuse_bulk_clear_with_relations` (per-file scoping, multi-task
  attribution, the `json_import` pseudo-source) and for `_removal_id_set`
  returning the whole subtree.

## Still open — E-1926 only

The FK-free tables (`session_tasks`, `session_hidden_tasks`, `session_notices`,
`project_next_tasks` / `_pending`) stay out. They are not relations, there is no
`unlink` to demand, and their schema comments say outliving the task is the
point — so the guard would be unclearable rather than merely strict. That needs
a decision about what a freed task id means, which is E-1926's job.

fields.outcome: Folded into E-1915's second landing rather than tracked separately — the guard is the same rule at a second call site (_refuse_bulk_clear_with_relations), and reuses _relations_referencing() from the first landing. `task import --replace` and `import-json --clear` now refuse while a relation references any task they would delete. No design call was needed: the objection (a bulk refresh refusing is more obstructive than one named removal) is answered by the message naming the file and the exact unlink, not by a weaker rule.

Folded into E-1915's second landing. Three-line fix reusing _removal_id_set() from the first landing: remove_item now computes the removal id set once before the emit and reports len(ids)-1, replacing the recursive query that ran after emit_event (which deletes the subtree synchronously) and so always counted 0.

# Plan — E-1893: require replies to restate the task IDs they are about

## Decisions (user, 2026-08-08)

Delivery surfaces: **handoff templates, the E-1919 output style, and `endless guide`**.
Explicitly NOT the E-1803 PostToolUse nudge — E-1911 just rewrote that nudge and parked
E-1901's enforcement arm, so it is recently-settled ground this task will not disturb.

The style's reach gap is closed two ways: activate it for endless now, and add a
**dim FYI on stderr** telling a *human* operator the style is installed but inactive.
Optional in principle; treated as required for any project using Endless for now.

## Part 1 — handoff templates (one sentence, one place)

The analysis's open question (a line in each of seven templates vs a shared fragment)
resolves itself: `internal/templatecmd/templates/handoff/_close.tmpl` already exists,
already holds the reporting instructions, and is already parsed into every handoff
template's set via `handoffPartialNames`. Add the rule to the `handoff_close` define.

Wording must cover the crux from the analysis — the subject is often NOT the session's
own task, so the tmux window title does not supply the missing ID:

> Name the explicit task ID(s) in the first sentence that makes a claim about a task —
> including tasks other than your own, where my window title tells me nothing.

Do NOT add it to `handoff_verify` / `handoff_nonverify`; those are about the verify
command, and duplicating the rule invites drift between copies.

## Part 2 — E-1919 output style

The style's `## Lead with the IDs` section already says to open with the bare
identifiers the answer concerns. It does not stress the other-tasks case, which the
analysis calls the crux. Strengthen that section only — do not restructure it.

Because the style file is embedded, the change is made in
`internal/outputstylecmd/templates/Endless.md.tmpl`, then re-materialized into
`.claude/output-styles/Endless.md` with `outputstyle install --force`. Both copies must
be committed; a stale committed copy would silently shadow the intent.

`tests/tasks/e-1919-verify.sh` section 8 asserts the style body's contract clauses. Add
an assertion for the other-tasks wording so this cannot regress.

## Part 3 — `endless guide`

Add the rule to the reporting guidance in the guide's orchestration/reporting section,
for sessions not started from a handoff. Keep it to the same one sentence used in
`_close.tmpl` — three surfaces carrying three paraphrases is how the rule drifts.

Re-run `just regenerate-guide` if the section map changes.

## Part 4 — activate the style for endless

Commit `"outputStyle": "Endless"` into the main checkout's tracked
`.claude/settings.json`. Verified safe: `just claude-settings-init` rebuilds each
worktree's settings from the committed copy's non-hook keys plus the working copy's,
replacing only `hooks` (justfile:381-385), so the key survives worktree regeneration
rather than being dropped.

Note this is a genuine behavior change for every endless session, which is why E-1919
made it opt-in. It is being opted into deliberately here, not by default.

## Part 5 — the dim FYI (human-only, stderr, appended)

**Trigger:** any `endless` command run by a human. Never when run by an agent.

**Detection already exists — twice.** `agent_help.is_claude_code_agent()` and
`task_cmd._running_under_agent()` are byte-identical (`CLAUDECODE == "1"`). Consolidate
onto `agent_help.is_claude_code_agent()` and delete the duplicate rather than adding a
third caller — same reasoning that folded `templatecmd` onto
`monitor.ProjectRootFromCwd` in E-1919.

**Behavior:**
- Fires only when `not is_claude_code_agent()`.
- Fires only when the project has the style file present but `outputStyle` unset (or set
  to something else) in `.claude/settings.json` — i.e. exactly the inert state
  `outputstyle install` warns about.
- Writes to **stderr**, dim, appended after the command's normal output, so it never
  corrupts stdout for pipes/`--json` consumers.
- One line. Not an error, not a non-zero exit.
- Suppressed when the project has no style file at all (nothing to activate) and when
  `.claude/settings.json` is unreadable.

**Wording:** dim, and it must name the activation route, since there is no
`/output-style` command:

> FYI: the Endless output style is installed but not active — `/config output-style=Endless`

**Throttle — mtime marker, not the DB.** An earlier draft of this plan said to reuse
`monitor.ShouldThrottle`. That is wrong: it is Go-side and DB-backed (queries the
`activity` table), so calling it from the Python CLI would mean a subprocess on every
`endless` invocation — unacceptable overhead for a one-line FYI. Python's
`task_cmd._bg_throttle_warn` is a *count* threshold, not a time throttle, so it is not
the shape either.

Use a marker file instead: `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/endless/outputstyle-fyi/<project>.stamp`.
Print only when the marker is absent or older than the interval, then touch it. No DB,
no subprocess, ~5 lines. Default interval 4 hours, overridable via
`.endless/config.json`. A missing/unwritable cache dir means print (fail open) —
suppressing the reminder silently is the worse failure.

Do NOT ship an unthrottled per-invocation nag; that is the noise that got E-1901's gate
parked.

**Placement:** a single hook in the Python CLI's result callback / group teardown so it
appends after any subcommand, rather than being pasted into individual commands.

## Verification

Fold into the existing suite per the one-command rule:
`esu && ./tests/tasks/e-1893-verify.sh`

Checks:
1. `handoff_close` renders the ID rule for every handoff type (todo, bugfix, research,
   epic, brainstorm, respawn) — asserts the shared partial actually reaches all of them.
2. The rule appears exactly once per rendered handoff, not once per template that
   includes a partial.
3. The style body carries the other-tasks wording.
4. The embedded template and the committed `.claude/output-styles/Endless.md` are
   byte-identical — catches a re-materialization that was forgotten.
5. `endless guide` output contains the rule.
6. The FYI fires with `CLAUDECODE` unset and a project in the inert state.
7. The FYI does NOT fire when `CLAUDECODE=1`.
8. The FYI does NOT fire when `outputStyle` is already `Endless`.
9. The FYI goes to stderr, not stdout: stdout of a `--json` command still parses.
10. The FYI does not change exit status.
11. Only one agent-detection helper remains in the Python source.

## Out of scope

- The E-1803 PostToolUse nudge (user decision).
- A `--global` output style install; E-1919's project-scoped decision stands. If the
  per-project activation proves too narrow across 50+ sessions, that is a separate
  change against E-1785, not this task.
- Any enforcement gate. This task delivers instructions on three surfaces plus one
  human-facing FYI; it deliberately adds no teeth.

payload.title: Orphaned relation rows are prevented by refusing the delete, not by cascading it
payload.description: task_deps and decision_relations carry no foreign key on their task endpoint — SQLite cannot express an FK whose target table varies by row — so a task delete leaves its relation rows behind, and reused task ids resurrect them as computed fact (E-1911's report claimed an unrelated E-1914 as a follow-up it filed). Enforce in application code, by REFUSING the delete and naming the unlink that clears each row. Deny rather than cascade: a severed relation is unrecoverable, a refusal costs one command. No per-type exemption — relates_to included; one rule that always holds beats a judgment call at the boundary. The guard belongs at every task-deleting verb, not only the one that prompted it: task remove was guarded first, and task import --replace was found orphaning rows the same way. reconcile() also repairs already-orphaned rows, but only while the freed id is unused — which is why prevention is primary. Governs relation rows only; the FK-free history tables are E-1926's question.

fields.description: From a bare (non-Claude) tmux pane inside a self-dev worktree, 'endless' (Python) and bare 'endless-go' silently run MAIN's code, so worktree changes cannot be exercised without PYTHONPATH=src or ./bin/endless-go, and new worktree flags error with 'No such option' until landed. Make bare invocations self-detect the worktree from cwd and re-exec the candidate build — the code-routing analog of the DB self-detection already shipped by E-1368/E-1281/E-1513. Approach is a gated, loop-guarded pre-parse self-re-exec reusing the existing worktree-path predicates; decisions and rationale were brainstormed in E-1687.
